title: Book 4, Chapter 12 — Seventh Year of the War—Occupation of Pylos—Surrender of the Spartan Army in Sphacteria
paragraphs: The next summer, about the time the corn was coming into ear, ten Syracusan ships and as many Locrian vessels sailed to Messina in Sicily. The inhabitants had invited them, and they occupied the town; Messina revolted from the Athenians. The Syracusans brought this about chiefly because they saw that the place gave access to Sicily, and feared that the Athenians might later use it as a base for attacking them with a larger force. The Locrians acted because they wished to make war from both sides of the strait and to reduce their enemies, the people of Rhegium. Meanwhile the Locrians had invaded Rhegian territory with all their forces, to stop the Rhegians from helping Messina, and also at the urging of some exiles from Rhegium who were with them. The long factions that had torn that town left it for the moment unable to resist, and this was a further temptation to the invaders. After devastating the country, the Locrian land forces withdrew; their ships stayed to guard Messina, while others were being manned to go to the same place and carry on the war from there.

About the same time, in the spring, before the corn was ripe, the Peloponnesians and their allies invaded Attica under Agis, son of Archidamus, king of the Lacedaemonians, and settled down to lay waste the country. Meanwhile the Athenians sent off to Sicily the forty ships they had been preparing, with the remaining generals Eurymedon and Sophocles; their colleague Pythodorus had already gone ahead. These generals were also instructed, as they sailed by, to look after the Corcyraeans in the town, who were being plundered by the exiles in the mountain. Sixty Peloponnesian vessels had lately sailed to support these exiles, in the belief that the famine raging in the city would make it easy to reduce. Demosthenes also had remained without employment since his return from Acarnania. He now applied for permission, and obtained it, to use the fleet if he wished on the coast of Peloponnese.

Off Laconia they heard that the Peloponnesian ships were already at Corcyra. Eurymedon and Sophocles then wished to hurry to the island, but Demosthenes required them first to touch at Pylos and do what was needed there before continuing their voyage. While they were still objecting, a squall came on and carried the fleet into Pylos. Demosthenes at once urged them to fortify the place, saying that this was why he had come on the voyage. He pointed out that there was plenty of stone and timber on the spot, that the place was strong by nature, and that it and much of the country round it were unoccupied. Pylos, or Coryphasium as the Lacedaemonians call it, is about forty-five miles from Sparta, in the old country of the Messenians. The commanders told him there was no lack of desert headlands in Peloponnese, if he wished to put the city to expense by occupying them. He thought, however, that this place was different from others of the kind because it had a harbor close by. The Messenians, the old natives of the country, spoke the same dialect as the Lacedaemonians, and could do them the greatest mischief by raids from it, while also serving as a trusty garrison.

He spoke to the captains of companies about it, but failed to persuade either the generals or the soldiers, and he remained inactive with the rest because of bad weather. Then the soldiers themselves, having nothing to do, were seized with a sudden impulse to go round and fortify the place. They set to work in earnest. They had no iron tools, so they picked up stones and fitted them together as they happened to match. Where mortar was needed, they carried it on their backs for lack of hods, stooping so that it would stay on and clasping their hands behind them to keep it from falling off. They spared no effort to finish the most vulnerable points before the Lacedaemonians arrived; most of the place was strong enough by nature without further fortification.

The Lacedaemonians, meanwhile, were celebrating a festival. At first they also made light of the news, thinking that whenever they chose to take the field the enemy would evacuate the place at once or be easily driven out by force; the absence of their army before Athens also had something to do with their delay. The Athenians fortified the place on the land side, and wherever it most needed it, in six days. They left Demosthenes with five ships to garrison it, and the main body of the fleet hurried on its voyage to Corcyra and Sicily.

The Peloponnesians in Attica heard of the occupation of Pylos and at once hurried home. The Lacedaemonians and their king Agis thought the matter concerned them closely. Besides, the invasion had begun early in the season, while the corn was still green, and most of their troops were short of provisions. The weather too was unusually bad for the time of year, and greatly distressed the army. Many reasons thus combined to hasten their departure and to make this a very short invasion: they stayed only fifteen days in Attica.

About the same time the Athenian general Simonides gathered a few Athenians from the garrisons and a number of the allies in those parts, and took Eion in Thrace by treachery. Eion was a Mendaean colony and hostile to Athens. But no sooner had he taken it than the Chalcidians and Bottiaeans came up and drove him out, with the loss of many of his soldiers.

When the Peloponnesians returned from Attica, the Spartans themselves and the nearest of the Perioeci set out at once for Pylos; the other Lacedaemonians followed more slowly, since they had just come in from another campaign. Word was also sent around Peloponnese to come up to Pylos as quickly as possible. The sixty Peloponnesian ships were sent for from Corcyra; their crews dragged them across the isthmus of Leucas, they passed unperceived by the Athenian squadron at Zacynthus, and they reached Pylos, where the land forces had arrived before them. Before the Peloponnesian fleet sailed in, Demosthenes found time to send out two ships unobserved, to tell Eurymedon and the Athenians on board the fleet at Zacynthus of the danger at Pylos and to summon them to his assistance. While the ships hurried on their voyage in obedience to his orders, the Lacedaemonians prepared to assault the fort by land and sea. They hoped to capture with ease a work built in haste and held by a feeble garrison. Meanwhile they expected the Athenian ships to arrive from Zacynthus, and intended, if they failed to take the place before then, to block the entrances of the harbor so that the Athenians could not anchor inside it. For the island of Sphacteria stretches in a line close in front of the harbor, making it safe and narrowing its entrances. It leaves a passage for two ships on the side nearest Pylos and the Athenian fortifications, and for eight or nine on the side toward the rest of the mainland. The island was entirely covered with wood, and since it was uninhabited it had no paths; it was about one mile and five furlongs in length. The Lacedaemonians meant to close the inlets with a line of ships placed close together, with their prows turned toward the sea. Meanwhile, fearing that the enemy might use the island to operate against them, they carried some heavy infantry over to it and stationed others along the coast. In this way the island and the continent would alike be hostile to the Athenians, who would be unable to land on either. The shore of Pylos itself, outside the inlet toward the open sea, has no harbor, and so offered no point the Athenians could use as a base to relieve their countrymen. The Lacedaemonians therefore would in all probability become masters of the place without a sea-fight or any risk, since it had been occupied on the spur of the moment and was unfurnished with provisions. This being determined, they carried over to the island the heavy infantry, drafted by lot from all the companies. Some others had crossed over before in relief parties, but those who were left there at the last numbered four hundred and twenty, with their Helot attendants, and were commanded by Epitadas, son of Molobrus.

Meanwhile Demosthenes, seeing that the Lacedaemonians were about to attack him by sea and land at once, was not idle himself. He drew up the galleys that remained to him, out of those that had been left him, under the fortification and enclosed them in a stockade. He armed the sailors taken from them with poor shields, most of them made of osier, since it was impossible to procure arms in such a desert place. Even these had been obtained from a thirty-oared Messenian privateer and a boat belonging to some Messenians who happened to have come to them. Among these Messenians were forty heavy infantry, whom he used along with the rest. He posted most of his men, unarmed and armed, at the best fortified and strongest points of the place toward the interior, with orders to repel any attack by the land forces. From his whole force he picked sixty heavy infantry and a few archers, and with these he went outside the wall down to the sea, where he thought the enemy would most likely attempt to land. The ground there was difficult and rocky, and faced the open sea. But this was the weakest part of the wall, and he thought that this fact would encourage the enemy’s ardor: the Athenians, confident in their naval superiority, had paid little attention to their defenses here, and the enemy, if he could force a landing, might feel sure of taking the place. Going down to the water’s edge at this point, he posted his heavy infantry to prevent a landing if possible, and encouraged them in the following terms:

“Soldiers and comrades in this adventure, I hope that in our present strait none of you will try to show his cleverness by reckoning up exactly all the perils around us. I hope you will instead hurry to close with the enemy, without stopping to count the odds, and see in this your best chance of safety. In emergencies like ours, calculation is out of place; the sooner we face the danger, the better. In my judgment, too, most of the chances are on our side, if only we stand fast and do not throw away our advantages out of awe at the enemy’s numbers. One point in our favor is the awkwardness of the landing. But this helps us only if we hold our ground. If we give way, the landing will be easy enough, in spite of its natural difficulty, because nobody will be there to stop it. And the enemy will at once become more formidable, since retreat will be harder for him — if we succeed in repulsing him, that is, which we shall find easier to do while he is still on board his ships than after he has landed and meets us on equal terms. As for his numbers, they need not alarm you too much. However large they are, he can engage only in small detachments, because many ships cannot bring to at once. Besides, we are not facing the numerical superiority of an army on land with everything else equal, but that of troops on board ship, on an element where many lucky chances are needed for them to act effectively. I therefore consider that his difficulties may fairly be weighed against our shortage of men. And I charge you, as Athenians who know from experience what it means to land from ships on hostile territory, and how impossible it is to drive back an enemy who is resolute enough to stand his ground and who is not frightened away by the surf and the terror of ships sailing in, to stand fast now, beat the enemy back at the water’s edge, and save yourselves and the place.”

Encouraged by these words of Demosthenes, the Athenians felt more confident, went down to meet the enemy, and took up positions along the edge of the sea. The Lacedaemonians now advanced and assaulted the fortification with their land forces and, at the same moment, with their ships, forty-three in number, under the admiral Thrasymelidas, son of Cratesicles, a Spartan. His attack came just where Demosthenes had expected it. The Athenians thus had to defend themselves on two sides, from the land and from the sea. The enemy rowed up in small detachments, each relieving the one before — many could not bring to at once — and showed great ardor, cheering each other on in the effort to force a passage and take the fortification. The man who distinguished himself most was Brasidas. He was captain of a galley, and he saw that the captains and steersmen, daunted by the difficulty of the position, were hanging back even where a landing seemed possible, for fear of wrecking their vessels. He shouted to them that they must not let the enemy fortify himself in their country just to save timber, but must shatter their vessels and force a landing. And he told the allies that in such a moment they must not hesitate: in return for the many benefits they had received from Lacedaemon, they must sacrifice their ships, run them boldly aground, get ashore one way or another, and make themselves masters of the place and its garrison.

Not content with this exhortation, he forced his own steersman to run the ship ashore. He stepped onto the gangway and was trying to land when the Athenians cut him down; after many wounds he fainted. He fell into the bows, and his shield slipped from his arm into the sea. It was washed ashore and picked up by the Athenians, who later used it for the trophy they set up for this attack. The rest also did their best, but could not land, because the ground was difficult and the Athenians held on without flinching. It was a strange reversal of the usual order of things. Athenians were fighting from the land, and Laconian land at that, against Lacedaemonians coming from the sea; and Lacedaemonians were trying to land from shipboard in their own country, now hostile, to attack Athenians. Yet at that time the Lacedaemonians were famous chiefly as an inland people, superior by land, and the Athenians as a maritime people with a navy that had no equal.

The Peloponnesians continued their attacks during that day and most of the next, and then desisted. The day after, they sent some of their ships to Asine for timber to make engines. With these they hoped to take, in spite of its height, the wall opposite the harbor, where the landing was easiest. At this moment the Athenian fleet from Zacynthus arrived, now numbering fifty ships, reinforced by some of the ships on guard at Naupactus and by four Chian vessels. They saw the coast and the island both crowded with heavy infantry, and the hostile ships in the harbor showing no sign of sailing out. At a loss where to anchor, they sailed for the moment to the desert island of Prote, not far off, where they passed the night. The next day they got under way, ready to engage in the open sea if the enemy chose to put out to meet them, and determined, if he did not, to sail in and attack him. The Lacedaemonians did not put out to sea. They had failed to close the inlets as they had intended, and they stayed quiet on shore, manning their ships and getting ready to fight in the harbor, which is a fairly large one, if anyone sailed in.

Seeing this, the Athenians advanced against them by each inlet. They fell on the enemy’s fleet, most of which was by this time afloat and in line, and put it to flight at once. They chased it as far as the short distance allowed, disabled a good many vessels and took five, one with its crew on board. They dashed in at the rest that had taken refuge on shore, and battered some that were still being manned before they could put out; they also lashed other, empty ships whose crews had fled to their own ships and towed them off. At this sight the Lacedaemonians, maddened by a disaster that cut off their men on the island, rushed to the rescue. They went into the sea with their heavy armor, laid hold of the ships and tried to drag them back, each man thinking that success depended on his own exertions. The melee was great, and quite contrary to the naval tactics usual to the two combatants. The Lacedaemonians, in their excitement and dismay, were actually fighting a sea-fight on land, while the victorious Athenians, in their eagerness to push their success as far as possible, were fighting a land-fight from their ships. After great exertions and numerous wounds on both sides, they separated. The Lacedaemonians saved their empty ships, except those first taken. Both parties returned to their camps, and the Athenians set up a trophy, gave back the dead, secured the wrecks, and at once began to cruise round the island and keep jealous watch on it, with its intercepted garrison. The Peloponnesians on the mainland, whose contingents had now all come up, stayed where they were before Pylos.

News of what had happened at Pylos reached Sparta. The disaster was thought so serious that the Lacedaemonians resolved to send the authorities down to the camp, to decide on the spot what was best to do. There they saw that they could not help their men, and they did not want to risk seeing them starved into submission or overpowered by numbers. So they determined, with the consent of the Athenian generals, to conclude an armistice at Pylos, send envoys to Athens to obtain a convention, and try to get their men back as quickly as possible.
The generals accepted their offers, and an armistice was concluded on the following terms:

That the Lacedaemonians should bring to Pylos, and deliver up to the Athenians, the ships that had fought in the late engagement and all the vessels of war in Laconia, and should make no attack on the fortification by land or by sea.

That the Athenians should allow the Lacedaemonians on the mainland to send over to the men on the island a fixed ration of ready-kneaded corn: two quarts of barley meal, one pint of wine and a piece of meat for each man, and half as much for a servant.
That the Lacedaemonians should send this allowance over in full view of the Athenians, and that no boat should sail to the island except openly.
That the Athenians should go on guarding the island as before, but without landing on it, and should not attack the Peloponnesian troops by land or by sea.
That if either party broke any of these terms in even the slightest particular, the armistice should be void at once.

That the armistice should remain in force until the Lacedaemonian envoys came back from Athens, the Athenians sending them there in a galley and bringing them back; that it should end on their arrival; and that the Athenians should then return the ships in the same condition in which they had received them.
Such were the terms of the armistice. The ships, sixty in number, were delivered over, and the envoys were sent off accordingly. When they arrived at Athens they spoke as follows:

“Athenians, the Lacedaemonians sent us to try to find a way of settling the matter of our men on the island, a way that will serve our interests and also protect our dignity in misfortune as far as circumstances allow. We can venture to speak at some length without breaking with the habit of our country. We are men of few words where many are not needed, but we can say more when there is an important matter to explain and some purpose to be served by explaining it. Meanwhile we ask you not to take what we say in a hostile spirit, nor as if we thought you ignorant and wished to lecture you. Take it rather as a suggestion about the best course to follow, put to intelligent judges. You can now, if you choose, turn your present success to advantage: you can keep what you have won and gain honor and reputation besides. You can avoid the mistake of those who meet with extraordinary good fortune and are led on by hope to keep reaching for more, because they have already succeeded beyond their expectation. Those who have known the most changes of good and bad fortune are also, rightly, the least trustful of their prosperity; and to teach your city and ours this lesson, experience has not been lacking.

“To be convinced of this, you have only to look at our present misfortune. What power in Hellas stood higher than we did? And yet we have come to you, although we once thought ourselves better able to grant what we are now here to ask. Nevertheless, our power has not decayed to bring us to this, nor did aggrandizement turn our heads. No, our resources are what they have always been, and what failed us was our judgment, a failing to which all are equally liable. So the prosperity your city now enjoys, and the strength it has lately gained, must not lead you to imagine that fortune will always be with you. Sensible men are prudent enough to treat their gains as precarious, just as they keep a clear head in adversity. They hold that war, far from staying within the limit a combatant may wish to set for it, will run the course its chances dictate. Not being puffed up by confidence in military success, they are therefore less likely to come to grief, and readiest to make peace, if they can, while their fortune lasts. This, Athenians, you have a good opportunity to do now with us. You can thus escape the disasters that may follow if you refuse, and the charge that even your present advantages were owed to accident, when you might have left behind a reputation for power and wisdom that nothing could endanger.

“The Lacedaemonians therefore invite you to make a treaty and end the war. They offer peace and alliance, and the most friendly and intimate relations between us in every way and on every occasion; and in return they ask for the men on the island. They think it better for both sides not to hold out to the end, in case some lucky accident lets the men break out, or the pressure of blockade forces them to give in. Indeed, if great enmities are ever to be truly settled, we think the settlement will come not through revenge and military success, and by forcing an opponent to swear to a treaty that works against him. It will come when the luckier combatant gives up these privileges, lets gentler feelings guide him, beats his rival in generosity, and grants peace on more moderate terms than the other expected. From that moment, instead of the debt of revenge that violence must bring, his adversary owes a debt of generosity to be repaid in kind, and honor inclines him to keep his agreement. Men also act in this way more often toward their greatest enemies than in quarrels of less importance. And they are by nature as glad to yield to those who first yield to them as they are prone to be provoked by arrogance into risks that their own judgment condemns.

“To apply this to ourselves: if peace was ever desirable for both sides, it surely is so now, before anything irremediable happens to us and makes us hate you forever, personally as well as politically, and makes you lose the advantages we now offer you. The outcome is still in doubt. You have reputation and our friendship in prospect, and we have the chance to compromise on our misfortune before anything fatal occurs. Let us be reconciled, and choose peace instead of war for ourselves, and give the rest of the Hellenes relief from their sufferings, for which, be sure, they will think they have chiefly you to thank. They do not know which side began the war they labor under, but the peace that ends it, since it depends on your decision, will be laid to your door by their gratitude. By such a decision you can become firm friends with the Lacedaemonians, at their own invitation, which you do not extort from them but oblige them by accepting. And consider the advantages likely to follow from this friendship: when Attica and Sparta are at one, the rest of Hellas, be sure, will remain in respectful inferiority before its heads.”

Such were the words of the Lacedaemonians. They thought that the Athenians, already wanting a truce and held back only by Lacedaemonian opposition, would gladly accept a peace freely offered, and give back the men. The Athenians, however, held the men on the island, and thought the treaty would be ready for them whenever they chose to make it; so they reached for something more. The first to encourage them in this policy was Cleon, son of Cleaenetus, a popular leader of the time with great power over the multitude. He persuaded them to reply as follows. First, the men on the island must surrender themselves and their arms, and be brought to Athens. Next, the Lacedaemonians must restore Nisaea, Pegae, Troezen and Achaia. These places had been won not by arms but by the previous convention, under which Athens herself had ceded them in a moment of disaster, when she needed a truce more than she did now. When this was done, the Lacedaemonians might take back their men, and make a truce for as long as both sides agreed.

The envoys made no reply to this answer. They asked instead that commissioners be chosen to confer with them on each point, so that they could talk the matter over quietly and try to reach some agreement. Cleon then attacked them violently. He said he had known from the start that their intentions were not honest, and that it was clear enough now, since they refused to speak before the people and wanted to confer in secret with a committee of two or three. No, he said, if they meant anything honest, let them say it out before everyone. The Lacedaemonians saw that, whatever concessions they might be ready to make in their misfortune, they could not speak before the multitude and lose credit with their allies over a negotiation that might still come to nothing. They saw, too, that the Athenians would never grant their request on moderate terms. So they returned from Athens having accomplished nothing.

Their arrival at once put an end to the armistice at Pylos, and the Lacedaemonians asked for their ships back, according to the convention. The Athenians, however, alleged an attack on the fort in violation of the truce, and other grievances that hardly seemed worth mentioning, and refused to give the ships back, insisting on the clause by which the slightest infringement made the armistice void. The Lacedaemonians denied the violation and protested against the Athenians’ bad faith over the ships. Then they went away and addressed themselves earnestly to the war. Hostilities at Pylos were now carried on vigorously by both sides. The Athenians cruised round the island all day with two ships going in different directions. By night, except on the seaward side in windy weather, they anchored round it with their whole fleet, which had been reinforced by twenty ships from Athens, come to aid in the blockade, and now numbered seventy ships. The Peloponnesians, meanwhile, remained encamped on the continent, making attacks on the fort and watching for any opportunity that might offer itself to deliver their men.

Meanwhile the Syracusans and their allies in Sicily had finished preparing the reinforcement we left them assembling, and had added it to the squadron guarding Messina. From there they carried on the war. The Locrians urged them on most, out of hatred for the Rhegians, whose territory they had invaded with all their forces. The Syracusans also wanted to try their fortune at sea. They saw that the Athenians had only a few ships actually at Rhegium, and they heard that the main fleet meant to join them was occupied in blockading the island. A naval victory, they thought, would let them blockade Rhegium by sea and land and reduce it easily. That success would at once put their affairs on a solid footing, since the promontory of Rhegium in Italy and Messina in Sicily lie so close together that the Athenians could not cruise against them and command the strait. The strait in question is the sea between Rhegium and Messina, at the point where Sicily comes nearest to the continent. It is the Charybdis through which the story has Ulysses sail. The narrowness of the passage, and the strength of the current pouring in from the vast Tyrrhenian and Sicilian seas, have rightly given it a bad reputation.

In this strait the Syracusans and their allies were forced to fight late in the day over the passage of a boat. They put out with rather more than thirty ships against sixteen Athenian and eight Rhegian vessels. The Athenians defeated them, and they hurried off, each for himself, to their own stations at Messina and Rhegium, having lost one ship; night came on before the battle was finished. After this the Locrians withdrew from the Rhegian territory, and the ships of the Syracusans and their allies joined together and anchored at Cape Pelorus, in the territory of Messina, where their land forces joined them. The Athenians and Rhegians sailed up and, seeing the ships unmanned, attacked. In this attack they in their turn lost one vessel, which was caught by a grappling iron, though the crew saved themselves by swimming. After this the Syracusans went on board their ships, and while they were being towed along the shore to Messina, the Athenians attacked them again. But the Syracusans suddenly put out to sea, became the attackers, and made the Athenians lose another vessel. They had held their own in the voyage along the shore and in the fighting just described, and they now sailed on into the harbor of Messina.

Meanwhile the Athenians had been warned that Camarina was about to be betrayed to the Syracusans by Archias and his party, and sailed there. The Messinese took the opportunity to attack their Chalcidian neighbor, Naxos, with all their forces by sea and land. On the first day they forced the Naxians to keep inside their walls and laid waste their country. On the next they sailed round with their ships and laid waste their land on the river Akesines, while their land forces threatened the city. Meanwhile the Sicels came down from the high country in great numbers to help against the Messinese. The Naxians were elated at the sight, and believed that the Leontines and their other Hellenic allies were coming to support them. They suddenly sallied out from the town, attacked and routed the Messinese, and killed more than a thousand of them. The rest suffered severely in their retreat home, for the barbarians attacked them on the road and cut off most of them. The ships put in to Messina and afterwards dispersed to their different homes. The Leontines and their allies, together with the Athenians, at once turned their arms against Messina, now weakened. The Athenians attacked with their ships on the side of the harbor, and the land forces on the side of the town. But the Messinese sallied out with Demoteles and some Locrians who had been left to garrison the city after the disaster. They suddenly attacked and routed most of the Leontine army, killing a great number. When the Athenians saw this, they landed from their ships, fell on the Messinese in their disorder, and chased them back into the town. Then they set up a trophy and withdrew to Rhegium. After this the Hellenes in Sicily continued to make war on each other by land, without the Athenians.

Meanwhile the Athenians at Pylos were still besieging the Lacedaemonians on the island, while the Peloponnesian forces on the continent stayed where they were. The blockade was very laborious for the Athenians because of the want of food and water. There was no spring except one in the citadel of Pylos itself, and that was not large, so most of them had to dig up the shingle on the beach and drink whatever water they could find. They also suffered from want of room, since they were encamped in a narrow space. As there was no anchorage for the ships, some of the men took their meals on shore in turn while the others lay at anchor out at sea. But what discouraged them most was the unexpectedly long time it took to reduce a body of men shut up on a desert island with only brackish water to drink. They had imagined it would take only a few days. The reason was that the Lacedaemonians had advertised for volunteers to carry ground corn, wine, cheese and any other food useful in a siege into the island. They offered high prices, and promised freedom to any of the Helots who succeeded. The Helots were therefore most eager to engage in this risky traffic. They set out from various parts of Peloponnese and ran in by night on the seaward side of the island. They were best pleased when they could catch a wind to carry them in. It was easier to elude the lookout of the galleys when the wind blew from the sea, because the galleys could not then anchor round the island. The Helots, for their part, had their boats valued at their price in money, and ran them ashore without caring how they landed, since they were sure to find the soldiers waiting for them at the landing places. But all who risked it in fair weather were taken. Divers also swam in under water from the harbor, dragging along by a cord, in skins, poppyseed mixed with honey and crushed linseed. At first these went unnoticed, but afterwards a lookout was kept for them. In short, both sides tried every possible contrivance, the one to throw in provisions and the other to prevent them from coming in.

At Athens, meanwhile, the news that the army was in great distress, and that corn was finding its way in to the men on the island, caused no small perplexity. The Athenians began to fear that winter would come and find them still engaged in the blockade. They saw that it would then be impossible to convoy provisions round Peloponnese. The country offered no resources in itself, and even in summer they could not send round enough. A place without harbors could no longer be blockaded, and the men would either escape because the siege was abandoned, or would watch for bad weather and sail out in the boats that brought in their corn. What alarmed them still more was the attitude of the Lacedaemonians. The Athenians thought they must feel themselves on strong ground not to send any more envoys, and they began to repent of having rejected the treaty. Cleon saw that he was regarded with disfavor for having stood in the way of the convention. He now said that their informants did not speak the truth. When the messengers recommended that, if the Athenians did not believe them, they should send commissioners to see for themselves, the Athenians chose Cleon himself and Theagenes as commissioners. Cleon realized that he would now be obliged either to say what the men he was slandering had already said, or to be proved a liar if he said the contrary. He saw that the Athenians were not altogether unwilling to make a fresh expedition, and told them that, instead of sending commissioners and wasting their time and opportunities, they ought to sail against the men if they believed what they were told. Then he pointed at Nicias, son of Niceratus, who was then general and whom he hated, and said tauntingly that it would be easy, if they had real men for generals, to sail with a force and take the men on the island. If he himself were in command, he said, he would have done it.

Nicias saw the Athenians murmuring against Cleon for not sailing now, if it seemed so easy to him. He saw too that he himself was the object of the attack, and he told Cleon that, as far as the generals were concerned, he might take whatever force he chose and make the attempt. At first Cleon took this resignation for a mere figure of speech and was ready to go. But when he found that it was meant seriously, he drew back. He said that Nicias, not he, was general, for he was now frightened, having never supposed that Nicias would go so far as to step down in his favor. Nicias, however, repeated his offer, resigned the command against Pylos, and called the Athenians to witness that he did so. And as a crowd is apt to do, the more Cleon shrank from the expedition and tried to back out of what he had said, the more they urged Nicias to hand over his command and clamored at Cleon to go. At last, not knowing how to get out of his words, Cleon undertook the expedition. He came forward and said that he was not afraid of the Lacedaemonians, and that he would sail without taking anyone from the city with him, except the Lemnians and Imbrians who were at Athens, some targeteers who had come up from Aenus, and four hundred archers from other quarters. With these and the soldiers at Pylos, he said, he would within twenty days either bring the Lacedaemonians back alive or kill them on the spot. The Athenians could not help laughing at his folly. Sensible men, however, comforted themselves with the thought that they must gain either way: either they would be rid of Cleon, which they rather hoped, or, if disappointed in that, they would reduce the Lacedaemonians.

When he had settled everything in the assembly and the Athenians had voted him the command of the expedition, he chose Demosthenes, one of the generals at Pylos, as his colleague, and pushed forward the preparations for the voyage. He chose Demosthenes because he heard that he was contemplating a descent on the island. The soldiers, distressed by the difficulties of their position and rather besieged than besiegers, were eager to fight it out, and the burning of the island had increased the general’s confidence. He had at first been afraid. The island had never been inhabited and was almost entirely covered with wood, without paths, and he thought this favored the enemy: he might land with a large force and still suffer loss from an attack out of an unseen position. The wood would in great measure hide the enemy’s mistakes and forces from him, while every blunder of his own troops would at once be detected, and the enemy could fall on him unexpectedly wherever they pleased, since the attack would always be in their power. If, on the other hand, he forced them to fight in the thicket, the smaller number who knew the country would, he thought, have the advantage over the larger number who did not. And his own army might be cut off unnoticed, in spite of its numbers, as the men would not be able to see where to help each other.

The Aetolian disaster, which had been mainly caused by the wood, had not a little to do with these reflections. Meanwhile one of the soldiers, who were compelled by want of room to land on the extremities of the island and take their dinners, with outposts posted to prevent a surprise, set fire to a little of the wood without meaning to. As it came on to blow soon afterwards, almost the whole wood was consumed before they were aware of it. Demosthenes was now able for the first time to see how numerous the Lacedaemonians really were, for up to this moment he had been under the impression that they took in provisions for a smaller number. He also saw that the Athenians thought success important and were anxious about it, and that it was now easier to land on the island. He accordingly got ready for the attempt, sent for troops from the allies in the neighborhood, and pushed forward his other preparations. At this moment Cleon arrived at Pylos with the troops he had asked for, having sent word ahead that he was coming. The first step the two generals took after meeting was to send a herald to the camp on the mainland. He was to ask whether the Lacedaemonians there were disposed to avoid all risk and to order the men on the island to surrender themselves and their arms, to be kept in gentle custody until some general convention should be concluded.

When this proposal was rejected, the generals let one day pass. The next day they embarked all their heavy infantry on a few ships and put out by night. A little before dawn they landed, about eight hundred strong, on both sides of the island, from the open sea and from the harbor, and advanced at a run against the first post on the island.

The enemy had distributed his force as follows. In this first post there were about thirty heavy infantry. The center and most level part of the island, where the water was, was held by the main body under Epitadas, their commander. A small party guarded the very end of the island toward Pylos, which was precipitous on the seaward side and very difficult to attack from the land. There was also a sort of old fort there, of stones roughly put together, which they thought might be useful to them if they were forced to retreat. Such was their disposition.

The advanced post thus attacked by the Athenians was put to the sword at once. The men were scarcely out of bed and still arming, for the landing had taken them by surprise: they had fancied that the ships were only sailing as usual to their stations for the night. As soon as day broke, the rest of the army landed. This was all the crews of rather more than seventy ships, except the lowest rank of oarsmen, with the arms they carried, eight hundred archers and as many targeteers, the Messenian reinforcements, and all the other troops on duty round Pylos, except the garrison on the fort. Demosthenes had divided them, as his tactics required, into companies of two hundred, more or less, and had them occupy the highest points. His aim was to paralyze the enemy by surrounding him on every side, leaving him without any tangible adversary and exposed to the cross-fire of their host. If he attacked in front, he would be plied by those in his rear, and if he moved against those on one flank, by those on the other. In short, wherever he went he would have assailants behind him, and these were light-armed assailants, the most awkward of all. Arrows, darts, stones and slings made them formidable at a distance, and there was no means of getting at them at close quarters, for they could conquer in flight, and the moment their pursuer turned they were upon him. Such was the idea that inspired Demosthenes in conceiving the descent, and that governed its execution.

Meanwhile the main body of the troops on the island, that under Epitadas, saw their outpost cut off and an army advancing against them. They closed their ranks and pressed forward to engage the Athenian heavy infantry in front of them, with the light troops on their flanks and rear. But they could not engage, or make use of their superior skill. The light troops kept them in check on either side with their missiles, and the heavy infantry stayed where they were instead of advancing to meet them. Wherever the light troops ran up and came too close, the Lacedaemonians routed them, yet the light troops retreated fighting. They were lightly equipped and easily got a start in their flight, because of the difficult and rugged ground, on an island hitherto desert, over which the Lacedaemonians could not pursue them in their heavy armor.

After this skirmishing had lasted some little while, the Lacedaemonians became unable to dash out with the same speed as before upon the points attacked. The light troops, finding that they now fought with less vigor, grew more confident. They could see with their own eyes that they were many times more numerous than the enemy. They were now more familiar with his appearance and found him less terrible, since the result had not justified the fears they had felt when they first landed, in slavish dismay at the idea of attacking Lacedaemonians. Their fear therefore changed to disdain, and they rushed all together upon the Lacedaemonians with loud shouts, and pelted them with stones, darts and arrows, whichever came first to hand. The shouting that accompanied their onset confounded the Lacedaemonians, who were unaccustomed to this mode of fighting. Dust rose from the newly burnt wood, and it was impossible to see ahead, with arrows and stones flying through clouds of dust from the hands of numerous assailants. The Lacedaemonians now had to sustain a rough conflict. Their caps would not keep out the arrows, darts had broken off in the armor of the wounded, and they themselves were helpless to strike back, because they could not use their eyes to see what was before them and could not hear the words of command for the uproar the enemy raised. Danger surrounded them on every side, and they had no hope of any means of defense or safety.

At last, after many had been wounded in the confined space in which they were fighting, they formed in close order and retired on the fort at the end of the island, which was not far off, where their friends held the post. The moment they gave way, the light troops became bolder and pressed upon them, shouting louder than ever. They killed as many as they came up with in the retreat, but most of the Lacedaemonians made good their escape to the fort. With the garrison there they ranged themselves along its whole extent, to repulse the enemy wherever it could be assailed. The Athenians pursued but, because of the strength of the ground, could not surround and hem them in. They attacked in front and tried to storm the position. For a long time, indeed for most of the day, both sides held out against all the torments of the battle, thirst and sun, the one trying to drive the enemy from the high ground, the other to maintain himself on it. It was now easier for the Lacedaemonians to defend themselves than before, as they could not be surrounded on the flanks.

The struggle began to seem endless, when the commander of the Messenians came to Cleon and Demosthenes and told them that they were wasting their labor. But if they would give him some archers and light troops to go round to the enemy’s rear by a way he would undertake to find, he thought he could force the approach. When he had received what he asked for, he started from a point out of sight, so as not to be seen by the enemy. He crept on wherever the precipices of the island permitted, and where the Lacedaemonians, trusting to the strength of the ground, kept no guard. After the greatest difficulty he succeeded in getting round without being seen, and suddenly appeared on the high ground in their rear. The surprised enemy were dismayed, and his waiting friends were still more overjoyed. The Lacedaemonians were thus placed between two fires, and in the same dilemma (to compare small things with great) as at Thermopylae, where the defenders were cut off when the Persians got round by the path. Attacked now in front and behind, they began to give way, and, overcome by the odds against them and exhausted from want of food, they retreated.

The Athenians were already masters of the approaches. Cleon and Demosthenes saw that if the enemy gave way a single step further, their own soldiers would destroy them, and they put a stop to the battle and held their men back. They wished to take the Lacedaemonians alive to Athens, and hoped that their stubbornness might relax on hearing an offer of terms, and that they might surrender and yield to the present overwhelming danger. Proclamation was accordingly made, asking whether they would surrender themselves and their arms to the Athenians, to be dealt with at their discretion.

When the Lacedaemonians heard this offer, most of them lowered their shields and waved their hands to show that they accepted it. Hostilities now ceased, and a parley was held between Cleon and Demosthenes and, on the other side, Styphon, son of Pharax. Epitadas, the first of the previous commanders, had been killed, and Hippagretas, the next in command, had been left for dead among the slain, though still alive, so that the command had devolved upon Styphon according to the law, in case anything happened to his superiors. Styphon and his companions said they wished to send a herald to the Lacedaemonians on the mainland, to ask what they should do. The Athenians would not let any of them go, but themselves called for heralds from the mainland. After questions had been carried backwards and forwards two or three times, the last man who crossed over from the Lacedaemonians on the continent brought this message: “The Lacedaemonians bid you decide for yourselves, so long as you do nothing dishonorable.” After consulting together, they surrendered themselves and their arms. The Athenians guarded them that day and night. The next morning they set up a trophy on the island and got ready to sail, giving their prisoners in batches to be guarded by the captains of the galleys. The Lacedaemonians sent a herald and took up their dead. The number of the killed and of the prisoners taken on the island was as follows. Four hundred and twenty heavy infantry had crossed over; three hundred all but eight were taken alive to Athens, and the rest were killed. About a hundred and twenty of the prisoners were Spartans. The Athenian loss was small, since the battle had not been fought at close quarters.

The blockade in all, counting from the fight at sea to the battle on the island, had lasted seventy-two days. For twenty of these, while the envoys sent to treat for peace were away, the men had been given provisions; for the rest they were fed by the smugglers. Corn and other food were found on the island, for the commander Epitadas had kept the men on half rations. The Athenians and Peloponnesians now each withdrew their forces from Pylos and went home. Crazy as Cleon’s promise was, he fulfilled it, bringing the men to Athens within the twenty days, as he had pledged himself to do.

Nothing that happened in the war surprised the Hellenes so much as this. It was the opinion that no force or famine could make the Lacedaemonians give up their arms; they would fight on as best they could, and die with them in their hands. Indeed, people could scarcely believe that those who had surrendered were of the same stuff as the fallen. An Athenian ally, some time afterwards, insultingly asked one of the prisoners from the island whether those who had fallen were men of honor. He received the answer that the atraktos — that is, the arrow — would be worth a great deal if it could tell men of honor from the rest. This alluded to the fact that the killed were those whom the stones and the arrows happened to hit.

When the men arrived, the Athenians determined to keep them in prison until the peace, and, if the Peloponnesians invaded their country in the interval, to bring them out and put them to death. Meanwhile the defense of Pylos was not forgotten. The Messenians from Naupactus sent some of their likeliest men to their old country, to which Pylos formerly belonged, and began a series of incursions into Laconia, which their common dialect made most destructive. The Lacedaemonians had hitherto had no experience of incursions or of warfare of this kind. They found the Helots deserting and feared the spread of revolution in their country, and they began to be seriously uneasy. In spite of their unwillingness to betray this to the Athenians, they began to send envoys to Athens and tried to recover Pylos and the prisoners. The Athenians, however, kept grasping at more, and dismissed envoy after envoy without their having achieved anything. Such was the history of the affair of Pylos.
